name: MCP Security and Authentication
blurb: Trust boundaries, credentials, and the failure modes.

points.desc: Remote MCP servers authenticate clients with OAuth 2.1: authorization-server discovery, dynamic client registration, and PKCE. Local stdio servers inherit the trust of the process that launched them instead.
points.name: Authorization is OAuth 2.1

points.desc: Every connected server can read what the client sends it and shape what the model sees in return. Connecting a server is granting it a capability, and the specification requires explicit user consent for tools and resources.
points.name: The trust boundary sits at the server

points.desc: A malicious server can carry instructions in tool names, descriptions, or results that try to steer the model - prompt injection by tool metadata. Clients are expected to show users what a tool will do before it runs.
points.name: Tool descriptions are attack surface

points.desc: The specification forbids passing a client's token through to upstream APIs and warns against proxy patterns where a server exercises a user's authority beyond what was consented.
points.name: Confused-deputy and token-passthrough failures

points.desc: Secrets flow through the authorization layer, never through model-visible text; a server that asks the model for a password is misdesigned by specification.
points.name: Credentials live with the user, not the model

reading.body:
The sharpest security risk in MCP is not the protocol itself but the trust a client implicitly extends the moment it connects to a server: every connected server can read client traffic and shape what the model sees, making server selection a security decision, not just a configuration one.

The specification draws a clear line between remote and local servers. Remote servers must authenticate clients using OAuth 2.1, with authorization-server discovery, dynamic client registration, and PKCE. Local stdio servers inherit the trust of whatever process launched them, which means their security depends entirely on the host environment rather than anything the protocol enforces.

Three failure modes receive explicit attention in the specification. First, tool metadata, including names, descriptions, and results, is attack surface: a malicious server can embed instructions there that attempt to steer the model, and clients are expected to show users what a tool will do before it runs. Second, confused-deputy and token-passthrough patterns are forbidden, because a server must not exercise a user's authority beyond what was consented. Third, credentials must flow through the authorization layer and never appear in model-visible text, so a server that prompts the model for a password is wrong by design, not just by practice.

The data covers the specification's stated requirements and named failure modes as of the date given. It does not cover how well deployed implementations follow those requirements, how clients verify tool descriptions before displaying them, or what happens when the authorization server itself is compromised.
